hypothesis: If a composition with five overlapping sound classes (for example, voice, percussion, bass, harmonic accompaniment, and environmental texture) is mixed through independent per-class gain controls updated in 6 ms streaming chunks, then listeners will identify and recall cues in a designated target layer more accurately, rate that layer as more clear, and report less masking-related fatigue than when the same material is controlled only by a single global attenuation or suppression parameter, because per-class mixing can reduce interference from specific competing sources without removing the entire surrounding soundscape.
question: Can independent real-time level control of up to five simultaneous musical sound classes improve listeners' ability to follow a designated musical layer while preserving a sense of richness and environmental immersion?
rationaleMd:
The source argues that conventional hearable controls are coarse: they generally provide global noise suppression or attention to one source rather than independently adjustable control over several simultaneous sources ([Claim 1]). Aurchestra instead produces separate streams for selected sound classes and allows independent per-class volume mixing ([Claim 2]). It is reported to support up to five overlapping target sounds ([Claim 3]) and to operate in real time using 6 ms streaming chunks ([Claim 4]).

A composition can operationalize these claims by constructing a five-class texture with deliberately competing spectral, rhythmic, and spatial materials. In a **global-control condition**, all non-target layers are attenuated together, mimicking coarse suppression. In an **independent-control condition**, only the classes that mask the current target are reduced, while non-masking layers remain audible. The dependent measures can include: (1) accuracy on target-cue detection or melodic/rhythmic recall, (2) response time to target-cue detection, (3) ratings of target clarity, immersion, and listening effort, and (4) preference for the resulting mix. Better target tracking without lower immersion in the independent-control condition would support the claim that fine-grained source control improves enhancement and interference suppression in complex real-world-like sound scenes ([Claim 5]).

sources.rawText: arXiv:2603.00395v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Hearables are becoming ubiquitous, yet their sound controls remain blunt: users can either enable global noise suppression or focus on a single target sound. Real-world acoustic scenes, however, contain many simultaneous sources that users may want to adjust independently. We introduce Aurchestra, the first system to provide fine-grained, real-time soundscape control on resource-constrained hearables. Our system has two key components: (1) a dynamic interface that surfaces only active sound classes and (2) a real-time, on-device multi-output extraction network that generates separate streams for each selected class, achieving robust performance for upto 5 overlapping target sounds, and letting users mix their environment by customizing per-class volumes, much like an audio engineer mixes tracks. We optimize the model architecture for multiple compute-limited platforms and demonstrate real-time performance on 6 ms streaming audio chunks. Across real-world environments in previously unseen indoor and outdoor scenarios, our system enables expressive per-class sound control and achieves substantial improvements in target-class enhancement and interference suppression. Our results show that the world need not be heard as a single, undifferentiated stream: with Aurchestra, the soundscape becomes truly programmable.
sources.title: Fine-grained Soundscape Control for Augmented Hearing

title: Five-Layer Adaptive Mixes and Perceived Musical Clarity
whyThisMatters: This tests whether source-separated, programmable mixing can become a compositional device rather than merely a hearing-assistance feature. If supported, composers could write denser five-layer works in which a listener's attention can be directed toward changing instrumental or environmental strata without sacrificing the complexity, spatial presence, and expressive contrast of the full arrangement. It would provide a measurable basis for composing adaptive headphone, hearable, or installation music whose foreground and background relationships can be personalized in real time.

details.interpretation: An RTF below 1 indicates faster-than-real-time synthesis under the reported evaluation conditions.

hypothesis: If identical 8–16 second musical prompts are rendered with a hierarchical latent-diffusion system using separate semantic and acoustic representations at 6.25 Hz, rather than a single highly compressed representation at 12.5 Hz, then listeners will rate the 6.25 Hz outputs as equal or higher in motif recognizability, instrument/source consistency, and phrase-level coherence, because separating semantic structure from acoustic detail reduces harmful latent-variable entanglement while retaining information needed for waveform reconstruction. The 6.25 Hz system should also achieve an RTF near or below 0.08.
question: Can a waveform-diffusion music generator operating with 6.25 Hz semantic-and-acoustic latents preserve perceived musical identity and phrase coherence as effectively as a 12.5 Hz compressed-latent system, while generating substantially faster?
rationaleMd:
The experiment compares two latent-rate conditions while holding the musical source material, duration, prompt content, output codec, and diffusion-sampling budget constant.

**Manipulations**
- Generate matched 8–16 second excerpts containing a clearly identifiable melodic motif, stable pulse, and one or two instrumental sources.
- Condition A: a 12.5 Hz highly compressed latent representation.
- Condition B: a 6.25 Hz latent-diffusion representation with distinct semantic and acoustic latent streams.
- Create prompt variations that independently alter: (1) melodic/rhythmic instruction, (2) instrumentation/timbre, and (3) production descriptors such as reverberant versus dry or soft versus distorted.
- Train each condition for the same one-day budget and measure inference speed as real-time factor.

**Observable outcomes**
- Blind listener ratings of motif recognizability: can listeners identify which reference motif generated excerpt variants derive from?
- Phrase-coherence ratings: do listeners perceive a stable beat, intelligible phrase boundaries, and continuous musical development?
- Source-consistency ratings: does an instrument or vocal-like source retain a consistent perceived identity across the excerpt?
- Prompt-adherence scores: do independently requested semantic changes and acoustic changes appear without unwanted changes to the other domain?
- Technical measures: RTF, onset/beat consistency, embedding similarity to the reference motif, and spectral/timbral consistency across phrase segments.

The source argues that regularization of intermediate diffusion-Transformer representations can entangle latent variables and constrain generation (**Claim 1**). For music, such entanglement may appear as unwanted coupling: asking for a new instrument might alter the melody, or changing rhythmic density might destabilize timbre. The proposed separated semantic/acoustic condition directly tests whether a hierarchy of representations reduces this coupling.

The feasibility of the comparison is supported by the report that ReGen improves waveform quality from highly compressed 12.5 Hz representations (**Claim 2**) and that a 6.25 Hz semantic/acoustic latent-diffusion configuration enables efficient training and fast inference (**Claim 4**). Although the reported evidence concerns speech, the claims of preserved intelligibility and identity at low rate (**Claim 3**) motivate analogous musical measures: motif recognizability functions as a musical counterpart to intelligibility, while stable instrument or performer character functions as a counterpart to speaker similarity.

A result in which 6.25 Hz semantic/acoustic latents match or exceed 12.5 Hz compressed latents on listener ratings, while approaching an RTF of 0.08, would support the hypothesis. Conversely, lower motif recognition, unstable instrumental identity, or reduced rhythmic continuity would indicate that the low-rate representation discards musical information not required for speech-oriented generation.

sources.rawText: arXiv:2607.09134v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Representation alignment (REPA) has been investigated to accelerate diffusion training, but we observe that regularizing intermediate representations in diffusion Transformers (DiT) may implicitly entangle latents and limit generative capacity. To address this issue, we propose ReGen, a hierarchical multi-prompt representation generation framework that jointly estimates multiple vector fields for both representations and data within a single diffusion model. We further introduce generalized flow matching (GFM) to improve the generalization of conditional flow matching (CFM). We validate ReGen on single-stage waveform diffusion models including neural audio codec and Wave-VAE. ReGen significantly improves waveform generation quality from highly compressed latent representations at 12.5 Hz. We also present ReGenVoice, a latent diffusion model (LDM)-based text-to-speech model that achieves strong speech intelligibility (WER) and speaker similarity (SIM) with a small dataset. Moreover, operating the LDM at 6.25 Hz with rich semantic and acoustic latent representation enables efficient training and sampling, requiring only 1 day of training on 4 GPUs and fast inference with an RTF of 0.08. Audio samples are available at https://regenvoice.github.io/demo/.
sources.title: ReGen: Hierarchical Multi-Prompt Representation Generation for Efficient Waveform Diffusion Models

title: Low-Rate Latents and Perceptual Coherence in Generated Musical Phrases
whyThisMatters: This tests whether very low temporal-resolution generation can become a compositional advantage rather than merely a computational compromise. If the hypothesis holds, composers could use fast, low-rate diffusion to generate and audition many coherent variations of a musical phrase—changing melody, rhythmic contour, instrumentation, or production character through prompts—without sacrificing the recognizability of the material. A positive result would support workflows in which semantic musical decisions and fine acoustic rendering are deliberately separated.

hypothesis: If a less-than-one-minute vocal composition systematically alternates sections with high voiced-feature activation (sustained vowels, sonorants, humming) and high nasal-feature activation (hums, /m/, /n/, /ŋ/-like articulations), separated by abrupt frame-level transitions into low-voicing consonantal or whispered material, then listeners will identify the transitions as clearer phrase boundaries and rate the sections as more texturally distinct than in a control version with matched pitch, rhythm, loudness, and duration but no structured phonological-feature contrast, because voicing and nasality are acoustically salient phonological dimensions that can be tracked frame by frame.
question: Can a vocal composition organized around frame-level changes in voicing and nasality produce reliably perceived phrase boundaries and contrasting vocal textures, even when listeners are not given linguistic transcriptions?
rationaleMd:
The source claims that phonetic structure is latent in self-supervised speech-model representations and can be used for phone segmentation and recognition (Claim 1). It further states that Phonological Activation Mapping (SPAM) maps each representation frame to phonological-feature activations, explicitly including **voicing** and **nasality** (Claim 2). These claims suggest that vocal audio contains temporally local, measurable feature trajectories that may correspond to perceptually meaningful changes.

The composition should therefore use frame-level feature activation as a control target: create one version whose vocal gestures are deliberately arranged into stable high-voicing/high-nasality regions and abrupt transitions, and a control version with the same macro-musical timing but more mixed or gradual feature values. Analyze both recordings with a self-supervised representation plus phonological-feature mapper, then compare listener judgments of boundary location, boundary strength, and vocal-texture contrast. The short duration is compatible with the source's report that the approach requires **less than one minute of phonetic transcription** for adaptation (Claim 3), making this feasible as a compact studio study. Reported strong segmentation performance across datasets (Claim 4) motivates treating activation discontinuities as candidate compositional boundaries.

sources.rawText: arXiv:2607.09020v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Phone segmentation and recognition are inherently related tasks, yet modern approaches typically model them separately. We argue that phonetic structure is already latent in the representations of self-supervised speech models (S3Ms), and one only needs to steer them to solve both tasks. We leverage S3M-based Phonological Activation Mapping (SPAM), which maps each S3M representation frame to a vector of phonological feature activations, such as voicing and nasality. On top of SPAM, we introduce two simple but effective lightweight, gradient-descent-free prediction heads: a recognition head and a segmentation head. Our method requires less than a minute of phonetic transcriptions, and generalizes to unseen phones during training. Across a diverse range of datasets, our approach attains strong segmentation and recognition performance.
sources.title: Phone Segmentation and Recognition through Phonological Activation Mapping

title: Phonological-Feature Mapping as a Compositional Control Layer
whyThisMatters: This tests whether machine-derived phonological features can function as musically useful compositional parameters rather than merely as speech-recognition labels. If supported, a composer could shape vocal form through trajectories of voicing and nasality: for example, using voiced/nasal continuity to create cohesion and abrupt feature changes to articulate cuts, entrances, and sectional boundaries. The result would provide a practical bridge between vocal-sound analysis and perceptually legible vocal composition without requiring conventional words or a large annotated corpus.

hypothesis: If cryptographic phase-bin watermarks are embedded identically across 10-second audio clips ranging from sparse sinusoidal tones (energy concentrated below 4 kHz) to spectrally dense broadband textures (energy distributed across the full 20 kHz range), then watermark survival rates after an 8 kHz low-pass filter attack will be significantly higher for the sparse-tone material, because those clips lose proportionally fewer watermark-carrying phase bins to the filter, while the dense textures lose the majority of their encoded phase structure — even though both clips began at perceptually equivalent PESQ scores near 3.02.
question: Does the perceptual transparency of STFT phase-bin watermarking (mean PESQ=3.02) hold equally across musical timbres with radically different spectral density profiles — such as sparse sine tones versus dense noise textures — and does the 8 kHz low-pass attack differentially destroy watermark integrity depending on how much musical energy lives above that cutoff?
rationaleMd:
## Rationale

### The Perceptual Transparency Baseline
Claim 1 establishes that pseudo-random STFT phase-bin manipulation achieves a **mean PESQ of 3.02**, implying listeners find phase-watermarked audio roughly equivalent in quality to the unwatermarked original. However, PESQ is an average over a test corpus — it does not tell us whether certain timbral classes are more or less sensitive. Sparse tonal material (e.g., a solo flute or sine wave) may expose phase artifacts more readily than broadband noise, or vice versa. The hypothesis targets this gap.

### The 8 kHz Low-Pass Attack as a Musical Variable
Claim 4 (personal observation) identifies **an 8 kHz low-pass filter on 44.1 kHz audio as among the most destructive signal-processing attacks on frequency-domain watermarks**, eliminating over 80% of the representable frequency spectrum. Crucially, this attack is not exotic — it approximates telephone codecs, lo-fi aesthetic processing, and certain streaming downsampling pipelines. For a sine-wave composition whose fundamental and harmonics all fall below 4 kHz, the filter removes nearly none of the musically relevant content *and* preserves the frequency bins where watermark phase data was encoded. For a broadband texture composition (white noise, metallic percussion, granular synthesis with components up to 20 kHz), the same filter aggressively culls the bins carrying encoded bits.

### Log-Magnitude Robustness as a Control
Claim 2 notes that **log-magnitude differences between adjacent frequency bins** survive lossy compression (MP3 and OGG-Vorbis at 128 kbps). This gives us a second encoding strategy to compare against pure phase manipulation: if log-magnitude encoding also fails under the 8 kHz attack for dense-spectrum material, the failure is structural (frequency bins are simply gone), not a phase-specific artifact.

### Redundant Temporal Distribution as a Partial Safeguard
Claim 5 suggests that phase watermarks are **distributed redundantly across the time-frequency representation**, surviving up to 20% end-cropping. This redundancy may partially compensate for frequency-domain losses in broadband material — but only if the redundancy is spread across frequency as well as time. If the watermarking scheme concentrates backup copies in specific frequency bands that also fall above 8 kHz, the redundancy offers no protection against a low-pass attack.

### Fragility of Detection-Only Approaches
Claim 3 warns that **passive forensic detectors for deepfake audio are sensitive to distribution shift** — they break when generative models evolve or when channel distortions are introduced. This strengthens the case for robust *embedded* watermarks over detection-based provenance. If our hypothesis confirms that timbral choices modulate watermark survival, it also implies that composers and audio engineers — not just cryptographers — are stakeholders in the design of robust provenance systems for generative audio.

### Experimental Design Sketch
- Generate 10-second clips at 44,100 Hz across a **spectral density gradient**: pure sine (440 Hz), harmonic cluster (below 4 kHz), broadband noise, and full-spectrum granular texture.
- Embed a 64-byte Ed25519 signature using STFT phase-bin encoding (matching the cryptographic payload from the paper's parameters).
- Apply three attacks: (a) 8 kHz low-pass filter, (b) 16 kHz round-trip resample, (c) MP3 at 128 kbps.
- Measure bit-error rate of recovered signature across timbral classes and attacks.
- Report PESQ before and after watermarking for each timbral class to check whether the PESQ=3.02 baseline holds across timbres.

sources.rawText: arXiv:2605.07241v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The proliferation of deepfake audio challenges voice-based authentication systems; passive forensic detectors are sensitive to evolving generative models and to real-world channel distortions. We propose Asymmetric Phase Coding (APC), a training-free cryptographic signing layer for audio, designed as a compact and auditable provenance primitive that can stand alone or be stacked with learned watermarks. APC combines Ed25519 digital signatures (EdDSA, FIPS 186-5; 64-byte signatures) with Reed-Solomon error correction, pseudo-random STFT phase-bin selection, and a redundant quantization-index-modulation (QIM) code on log-magnitude differences of adjacent bin pairs, yielding a compact, non-repudiable, blind-extractable watermark. We evaluate APC on 1,000 LibriSpeech test-clean clips (10 s each, 44.1 kHz) under eight attack configurations -- identity, 10% end-cropping, 20% end-cropping, 8 kHz low-pass, 16 kHz round-trip resampling, FLAC re-encoding, MP3 at 128 kbps, and OGG-Vorbis at 128 kbps -- and achieve cryptographic verification rates between 97.5% and 98.3% on every condition at mean PESQ=3.02 and tens-of-milliseconds CPU latency. We explicitly compare APC against recent neural baselines (AudioSeal, WavMark, SilentCipher), detail the threat model (forgery resistance vs. erasure), characterize the dataset, define all metrics, quantify an adaptive white-box erasure attack, and release code, keys, and metadata for reproducibility.
sources.title: Asymmetric Phase Coding Audio Watermarking

title: Phase-Domain Watermarking Across Timbre: Perceptual Transparency vs. Spectral Density
whyThisMatters: If this holds, it means that musical register and timbral density are not neutral parameters for composers working with authenticated or signed audio. A composer embedding provenance signatures into generative or AI-assisted music would need to make deliberate low-register, spectrally sparse arrangements if they want cryptographic integrity to survive broadcast or streaming pipelines that apply low-pass filtering or lossy compression. Conversely, composers working in noise, drone, or high-frequency texture genres (who naturally saturate the upper spectrum) would find their signed audio most vulnerable to authentication failure — not because of poor watermarking, but because of their aesthetic choices. This reframes timbre selection as a form of information-security decision-making, which has never been a design criterion in traditional composition practice.
